Family Health

How long does genital wart treatment take?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Genital warts are treatable, but the time needed varies. The most useful plan separates removing visible warts, allowing the skin to heal and reducing the chance of passing HPV on. A sexual health clinician can help you choose an option that fits the location of the warts and your health.

There is no single treatment timetable

Genital wart treatment often takes weeks or months. A procedure may remove visible warts in one visit, while a medicine applied at home works gradually over repeated applications. Healing after removal is another part of the timeline. Neither an immediate change in appearance nor finishing a prescription proves that HPV can no longer be passed on.

Response depends on the number, size and location of the warts, the chosen treatment, immune health and whether the treatment can be used as directed. Many warts respond within roughly three months, but some need a different approach. Ask the clinic when it expects to review progress and what should happen if there is little improvement.

What genital warts look like and how they are diagnosed

Genital warts are growths caused by certain types of human papillomavirus, or HPV. They may be skin-coloured, pink, flat, raised or clustered, sometimes with a cauliflower-like surface. They can affect the external genitals, groin, skin around the anus and, in some people, internal genital or anal sites. Itching, discomfort or bleeding can occur, although many warts are painless.

A clinician usually diagnoses them by examination. Not every lump in these areas is a wart. A dark, hard, ulcerated, bleeding or fixed lesion, an uncertain diagnosis, or a growth that does not respond as expected may need a biopsy. A routine HPV test is not used to confirm a visible genital wart. Internal lesions require the appropriate examination and specialist treatment.

Removing warts and controlling HPV are different

Treatment removes visible growths and can relieve physical symptoms and distress. It is not a medicine that reliably eliminates every trace of HPV. In many people the immune system brings the infection under control and HPV becomes undetectable within one to two years. Some infections persist or become detectable again later.

That does not mean everyone will have lifelong visible warts. It also does not allow a fixed date when an individual is certainly no longer infectious. A negative result, where HPV testing is indicated for another reason, and disappearance of a wart are different measurements. Follow the treatment and screening plan recommended for your circumstances rather than repeatedly testing to prove a complete cure.

Wart-causing types are usually different from cancer-causing types

Most genital warts are caused by HPV types 6 and 11, which are considered low-risk types. Persistent infection with other, high-risk HPV types is associated with cervical and some other cancers. Having an ordinary genital wart does not mean that you have cancer or that the wart will inevitably turn into cancer.

A person can have more than one HPV type, so wart treatment does not replace cervical screening when it is due. Warts alone do not generally require more frequent cervical screening. Unusual growths or bleeding still deserve assessment, especially with a weakened immune system. A clinician can explain which examination or test is relevant without treating every HPV infection as the same condition.

Why warts can return

Warts may recur after treatment, particularly during the first few months. This can reflect ongoing infection in nearby skin rather than a new sexual exposure. HPV may have been acquired months or years before a wart becomes visible, so the timing cannot reliably identify who passed it on or establish infidelity.

Previous infection does not guarantee lasting protection against the same type, and it does not protect against every other HPV type. If a growth returns, have it checked and discuss a new treatment plan. Repeatedly applying stronger products or increasing the frequency yourself can injure skin without resolving the reason for recurrence.

What the often-quoted reinfection study actually found

A 2017 study used mathematical models fitted to follow-up data from unvaccinated men. For HPV16, the model estimated that previous infection was associated with a roughly twentyfold higher probability of subsequent infection at one year and a fourteenfold higher probability at two years. Increased detection also occurred in men reporting no sexual activity.

These are relative model estimates for a particular HPV type and study population, not a percentage chance that your treated warts will return. HPV16 is mainly discussed in relation to cancer risk, rather than being a usual wart-causing type. The authors considered reactivation or transfer from another infected body site as possible explanations; the findings do not prove that every recurrence was a new infection from a partner.

Choosing treatment or a period of observation

Some untreated warts disappear, while others remain or grow in number or size. After confirming the diagnosis, a clinician may offer observation if symptoms and circumstances allow. Treatment may be preferable for discomfort, troublesome growths or the effect on your wellbeing. There is no single option that is best for every person.

Discuss the location of the warts, pregnancy possibility, immune conditions, cost, clinic access and how comfortable you are applying a medicine at home. The clinician should identify exactly which growths to treat. Do not use ordinary pharmacy treatments intended for hand or foot warts on genital skin, and do not attempt cutting, burning or freezing a lesion yourself.

Podofilox or podophyllotoxin

Podofilox, also called podophyllotoxin, destroys wart tissue and is used on selected external warts. Products and names vary between countries. Treatment typically alternates short application periods with days off so the skin can recover. Your prescription should specify the exact product, treated area, frequency and maximum number of cycles.

It is not an instruction to apply the medicine at least a certain number of times or continue indefinitely. More can cause more injury. Local burning, pain, irritation or erosion can occur, and normal surrounding skin should be protected according to the instructions. This medicine must not be used during pregnancy. Podophyllin resin is a different preparation and should not be substituted or used as a home remedy.

Imiquimod

Imiquimod helps stimulate a local immune response. Different strengths have different schedules and maximum courses: for example, the CDC lists courses of up to sixteen weeks for 5% cream and up to eight weeks for 3.75% cream. These are upper limits for those regimens, not a requirement that everyone use a cream for at least four months.

Follow the prescribed application and wash-off instructions rather than transferring directions from another strength. Redness, itching, burning, swelling, surface breakdown and changes in skin colour can occur. Contact the prescriber if the reaction is severe or makes the medicine difficult to use. Tell them about inflammatory skin conditions and any pregnancy possibility before treatment begins.

Sinecatechins

Sinecatechins is a standardized green-tea-extract ointment used for selected external genital or perianal warts. A plant origin does not make it the same as applying tea or a homemade herbal preparation. The prescribed course ends when clearance is achieved or the product’s maximum duration is reached; the CDC regimen does not continue beyond sixteen weeks.

Pain, itching, burning, swelling, redness and ulceration are possible. Avoid sexual contact while the ointment is on the skin and follow the product instructions about barriers such as condoms. It should not be used during pregnancy. Its safety and effectiveness are not established for some groups, including people with significant immune suppression, so suitability needs individual assessment.

Cryotherapy

Cryotherapy uses controlled freezing, usually with liquid nitrogen, to destroy wart tissue. It is performed by a trained clinician and may need several visits. The number and spacing of treatments depend on response and how the skin heals. A larger treatment area may need local anaesthetic.

Pain, soreness and blistering can follow freezing. Ask how to clean the treated area and when to seek advice. Do not assume that any discharge for several weeks is normal: worsening pain, fever, spreading redness, offensive discharge or difficulty passing urine should be checked. Combining freezing with another treatment is sometimes considered, but it is not automatically necessary or proven best for everyone.

Electrosurgery and removal with instruments

Electrosurgery uses electrical energy to destroy wart tissue. A clinician may also remove a growth with a small blade, scissors or curettage after numbing the area. These approaches can remove many visible warts at one visit, although new or residual warts can still need further treatment.

They should not be described as a fixed six-week course with a guaranteed clearance percentage. Anaesthesia, recovery and the need for repeat treatment depend on the extent and location. Bleeding, infection, scarring or changes in pigmentation are possible. Allow the treated skin to heal as instructed rather than seeking another destructive treatment before it has recovered.

Laser and other clinic treatments

Laser treatment may be considered for extensive, difficult-to-reach or treatment-resistant warts. The procedure and anaesthetic are selected for the area involved. Healing can take time, and the clinic should give specific wound-care and activity instructions. Laser is not a guarantee that HPV or future warts have been eliminated.

Some clinics use carefully applied trichloroacetic or bichloroacetic acid. These are concentrated medical treatments that can damage surrounding tissue if used incorrectly, not household acids to try yourself. Cervical, vaginal, urethral and internal anal warts need site-specific care; a product suitable for an external wart must not simply be placed internally.

Pregnancy and a weakened immune system change the plan

Tell the treating team if you are pregnant, might be pregnant or are trying to conceive. Podofilox, podophyllin and sinecatechins should not be used in pregnancy. Imiquimod is generally avoided because human pregnancy data remain limited. A clinician may choose a procedure or defer some treatment according to symptoms and the stage of pregnancy.

People with HIV or another cause of immune suppression can have larger, more persistent or recurrent warts. They may need closer follow-up and assessment of atypical lesions. This is not a reason to abandon treatment or assume cancer; it is a reason to tailor care and coordinate it with the team managing the underlying condition.

Sex, partners and the limits of a waiting period

Avoid sexual contact involving the affected area while warts are being treated and until the skin has healed, following your clinic’s instructions. Medicines on the skin can irritate a partner, and some preparations weaken condoms or diaphragms. There is no universal two-week countdown after the last wart disappears that proves transmission risk is zero.

Tell current partners about the diagnosis so you can discuss examination, other STI testing and prevention together. Routine HPV testing of partners for genital warts is not recommended. Condoms reduce exposure but do not cover every area of skin that can carry HPV. Choose intimacy that is comfortable for both people and do not continue through pain or broken skin.

Prevention and a practical follow-up plan

HPV vaccination helps prevent new infections with covered types; it does not treat existing warts. A previous HPV infection does not necessarily remove the benefit of vaccination against types not yet acquired. Eligibility and the number of doses depend on age, immune status, previous doses and local guidance. Ask a vaccination service rather than assuming everyone needs the same schedule.

Stopping smoking can support treatment response and overall health. No supplement, alcohol rule or immune-boosting product can promise clearance. Before leaving the clinic, confirm when to return, which side effects require a call and what to do if treatment has not helped by the end of its planned course. Change the plan with your clinician rather than extending it yourself.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Guidelines distinguish wart removal from eradication of HPV and do not identify one treatment as best for every patient.

Product strength, site, pregnancy and immune health affect treatment choice and timing; recurrence does not establish a recent exposure.

How BeMama can help

Write down the exact product, course limit and review date so you can ask for a change in treatment without guessing or overapplying it.

When to seek help

New genital growths need a diagnosis. Seek prompt advice for an atypical or bleeding lesion, severe treatment reaction, fever or difficulty urinating.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Treatment may take weeks or months, even when some visible warts can be removed in one visit.
  • A disappearing wart does not prove that transmission is impossible.
  • Follow the instructions for your exact prescription, not a generic timetable.
  • Vaccination prevents covered infections; it does not clear an existing wart.

Frequently asked questions

Is HPV always a lifelong visible condition?

No. Most new infections become undetectable over time, and many people never develop visible warts. Some infections persist or reactivate. Treatment cannot give an individual a guaranteed date when all HPV is gone.

Does a genital wart mean I have cancer?

Usually not. Typical genital warts are generally caused by low-risk HPV types. Atypical growths still need assessment, and cervical screening remains important when due.

Do I have to use imiquimod for four months?

Not necessarily. Duration depends on the strength, prescription and response. Some regimens have a maximum of sixteen weeks and others eight weeks; these are not minimum durations for everyone.

Can I apply more medicine to finish sooner?

No. Extra applications can injure normal skin. Follow the prescribed dose, area, rest days and maximum course, and ask the clinic what to do if progress is slow.

Will laser or electrosurgery cure HPV in one visit?

A procedure may remove visible warts in one visit, but it cannot guarantee that HPV has been eliminated or that warts will not recur. Healing and follow-up still matter.

Is sex safe exactly two weeks after the warts disappear?

There is no such guarantee. Follow the clinic’s healing and treatment advice. HPV can be transmitted after visible warts are gone, and condoms reduce rather than eliminate that risk.

Does a recurrence prove my partner recently passed it back?

No. HPV can persist or become detectable again, and warts can appear long after acquisition. A recurrence cannot identify when infection happened or prove infidelity.

Can I use a normal pharmacy wart remover?

No. Products for hand or foot warts can damage genital tissue. Have the lesion assessed and use a treatment specifically prescribed for its location.

What if I become pregnant during treatment?

Contact the prescriber promptly before further use so the medicine and plan can be reviewed. Several wart treatments are unsuitable in pregnancy. An exposure does not by itself establish harm, but it needs individual advice.

Should my partner get an HPV test?

Routine HPV testing of a partner for genital warts is not recommended. They may benefit from an examination, appropriate testing for other STIs and a discussion of vaccination.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
